messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: variability of an effect
parts:
I have estimates of the distribution of an effect across K groups, where
K is small, like 3. The overall goal is to get an estimate of the the
variability of the effect across groups. For each set of coefficients,
call it B_j for the j'th set, g_kj is the group effect for the k'th group.

One can compute the variance of g across k for each j, and have a
posterior distribution for the variance.

Should the individual variances use K or K-1 as the divisor? If B_j
actually were the correct coefficients it seems to me K would be more
appropriate--although I suppose even in that case we are still
estimating g_kj since we only have a sample of the target population k.

I'm also planning on using the range of the g_kj across k as a measure
of dispersion.

It's possible the whole strategy is misconceived; if so, let me know :)

I have managed to convince my colleagues that test of the null
hypothesis that all effects are equal is neither possible nor desirable
(or at least, that it's not possible). These other measures are an
effort to come up with a more useful, and more Bayesian, alternative.

These are estimates of variability of effects, not of variability in the
original model parameters, and so there is no variance parameter in a
hierarchical model that corresponds to the effects.

One other wrinkle is that the group effects are themselves aggregations
of individual effects. So we start with estimates of the individual
effects, d_ij, for individual i under coefficient set j. g_kj is the
mean of the d_ij for the subset of i in group k.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] variability of an effect
parts:
On May 30, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:

> I have estimates of the distribution of an effect across K groups, where K is small, like 3. The overall goal is to get an estimate of the the variability of the effect across groups. For each set of coefficients, call it B_j for the j'th set, g_kj is the group effect for the k'th group.
>
> One can compute the variance of g across k for each j, and have a posterior distribution for the variance.
>
> Should the individual variances use K or K-1 as the divisor?

> If B_j actually were the correct coefficients it seems to me K would be more appropriate--although I suppose even in that case we are still estimating g_kj since we only have a sample of the target population k.

The point would be to assume the K you observe are part of
some larger population you're trying to estimate. In
that case, 1/K yields the maximum likelihood estimator and 1/(K-1)
an unbiased estimator.

I would think the variance across groups would be very sensitive
to the priors you're using unless there's a lot of data per group.
> I'm also planning on using the range of the g_kj across k as a measure of dispersion.

Tail measures like 95% intervals are hard to estimate and require many more
samples.

>
> It's possible the whole strategy is misconceived; if so, let me know :)

I see you mention below you can't do a hierarchical model. I didn't
understand why. That'd be the usual approach, and then you can read off
the variance from there and it'll also determine the amount of pooling.
> I have managed to convince my colleagues that test of the null hypothesis that all effects are equal is neither possible nor desirable (or at least, that it's not possible).

It's not possible from a Bayesian perspective, because that's
a measure-zero event. You can measure usual event probabilities
like Pr(theta[1] > theta[2]) and the like.

Again, I'm not sure why you're not setting up a hierarchical model.

The prior variance is going to determine how much pooling
you do (all effects are equal is complete pooling, each
estimated independently is no pooling, which is presumably what
you're doing).

> These other measures are an effort to come up with a more useful, and more Bayesian, alternative.

> These are estimates of variability of effects, not of variability in the original model parameters, and so there is no variance parameter in a hierarchical model that corresponds to the effects.
What is the prior on the parameters you're using?

> One other wrinkle is that the group effects are themselves aggregations of individual effects. So we start with estimates of the individual effects, d_ij, for individual i under coefficient set j. g_kj is the mean of the d_ij for the subset of i in group k.

You mean g is literally calculated as a data mean?

- Bob

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] variability of an effect
parts:
On 5/30/2014 11:28 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On May 30, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:
>
>> I have estimates of the distribution of an effect across K groups, where K is small, like 3. The overall goal is to get an estimate of the the variability of the effect across groups. For each set of coefficients, call it B_j for the j'th set, g_kj is the group effect for the k'th group.
>>
>> One can compute the variance of g across k for each j, and have a posterior distribution for the variance.
>>
>> Should the individual variances use K or K-1 as the divisor?
>> If B_j actually were the correct coefficients it seems to me K would be more appropriate--although I suppose even in that case we are still estimating g_kj since we only have a sample of the target population k.
> The point would be to assume the K you observe are part of
> some larger population you're trying to estimate. In
> that case, 1/K yields the maximum likelihood estimator and 1/(K-1)
> an unbiased estimator.

The categories here are ethnic groups. Taking them (the categories, not
the individuals in them) as part of a larger population of categories
seems unnatural. The division into 3 includes most groups (whites being
the notable exception), and there is another division into 5 racial
categories that completely partitions the space ("other" is one of the 5
categories). The 3 categories are a subset of the 5 categories, and so
are part of a slightly larger (but far from infinite) population. But
the 5 aren't part of anything larger.

The racial/ethnic groups are themselves social constructs, and the
degree of refinement---saying that there is a group that is Latino as
opposed to separate groups for each country or separate groups for
Latino based on skin color---it itself an analytic decision rather than
a feature of nature.

>
> I would think the variance across groups would be very sensitive
> to the priors you're using unless there's a lot of data per group.
If you mean observed data, we have several hundred per ethnic group.

>> I'm also planning on using the range of the g_kj across k as a measure of dispersion.
> Tail measures like 95% intervals are hard to estimate and require many more
> samples.

The range doesn't seem much like a tail measure, at least if K is low.
The g are already averages, and I would think the distribution of
differences between them has more to do with the fat part of the
distributions. We do have some situation with 15 (3x5) categories, and
the maximum difference statistic seems more problematic there.

Concretely, suppose we knew that African-American (AA) respondents with
Asian/Pacific Islander (API) partners had a 50% chance of having risky
sex and all 14 other combinations had a 30% chance of risky sex. The
variance of the respondent x partner interaction is modest in this case,
and if we did a frequentist test for the equality of all effects it
would likely come out with "data consistent with the null" for samples
that weren't too big. Despite low variance and unimpressive p, I would
consider the interaction important in this case. That's the kind of
thing I'm trying to capture with the range statistic.

>
>> It's possible the whole strategy is misconceived; if so, let me know :)
> I see you mention below you can't do a hierarchical model. I didn't
> understand why. That'd be the usual approach, and then you can read off
> the variance from there and it'll also determine the amount of pooling.

The effect estimates are the results of simulations that use
hierarchical models. The input models are hierarchical, but the output
effect estimates are a result of a complicated transformation of those
inputs. The effect estimates are model outputs, not data inputs.

Are you suggesting treating the draws from the posterior as "data"
inputs to a hierarchical model?

What I meant, more precisely, is that the hierarchical models I have are
not directly models of effects, and so the variance parameters in them
do not translate directly to the variance of effects.

>
>> I have managed to convince my colleagues that test of the null hypothesis that all effects are equal is neither possible nor desirable (or at least, that it's not possible).
> It's not possible from a Bayesian perspective, because that's
> a measure-zero event. You can measure usual event probabilities
> like Pr(theta[1] > theta[2]) and the like.
>
>
> Again, I'm not sure why you're not setting up a hierarchical model.
>
> The prior variance is going to determine how much pooling
> you do (all effects are equal is complete pooling, each
> estimated independently is no pooling, which is presumably what
> you're doing).
>
>> These other measures are an effort to come up with a more useful, and more Bayesian, alternative.
>> These are estimates of variability of effects, not of variability in the original model parameters, and so there is no variance parameter in a hierarchical model that corresponds to the effects.
> What is the prior on the parameters you're using?

The input models have lots of terms that are interactions between the
categories (respondent race) and covariates. Typically the individual
parameter estimates were from a model in which they had a normal(0,
sigma) distribution with sigma~cauchy(0, 5). Different degrees of
interaction had different sigmas. The effects are the result of all the
interactions (in all relevant models) and the distribution of the input
covariates.

>
>> One other wrinkle is that the group effects are themselves aggregations of individual effects. So we start with estimates of the individual effects, d_ij, for individual i under coefficient set j. g_kj is the mean of the d_ij for the subset of i in group k.
> You mean g is literally calculated as a data mean?

It is the mean of the individual simulated effects. I wouldn't call the
effects data. The effect estimates for individuals, d_ij, are
themselves estimates of the mean effect for that individual, rather than
simply differences in simulated outcomes. For example, in estimating an
effect on a binary outcome, d_ij is the expected change in the
probability of the outcome between two scenarios given by an
intervention for individual i.

Ross
